extracted.intended_audience: publishers, authors, lawyers, and scholars interested in copyright law
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and case law about what kinds of literary, artistic, and practical works may be copyrighted, and the limits of that protection (titles, reports, newspapers, plays, music, pictures, maps, lectures, importers' liability, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in law reports (reporters' rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The court opinion itself is official work and 'cannot be copyrighted in the reporter's behalf' but a report contains 'matters auxiliary to the opinion' (syllabus, narrative of facts, condensed statement of arguments, foot-notes) the preparation of which involves literary labor and skill and which may be subject to copyright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases: Majority of law reports compiled with intent to obtain copyright; judge considered whether editors had in fact used reporter's work when rival issued condensed edition and decided in favor of the reporter. Contrast: a decision held that head-notes 'furnished to him by the judges as part of their official duty' could not be claimed by the reporter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper copyright eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Although statutes mention 'books' rather than 'newspapers,' a newspaper may be copyrighted under a liberal understanding of 'book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In a Beaconsfield memoir case the judge 'decided ... that the "Times" newspaper can be copyrighted' and that it should have been in order to sustain a claim. Alternate argument: publisher may claim a 'common-law right' independent of statute, but courts have varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in factual compilations and guide-books
rubrics_metrics.description: Guide-books and compilations of factual information are proper subjects of copyright, but the right is not so broad as to forbid others from collecting similar information or arranging it similarly; protection extends to copying 'material portions' of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In suit between Monitor Guide and Mackey's Shippers' Guide the judge said the right did not forbid Mackey from collecting similar information or arranging it in similar general ways, but only from 'copying material portions of the Monitor Guide.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for mechanically-used books vs patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Books designed for mechanical use (account-books, bond-registers, etc.) raise the question whether copyright or patent is the appropriate protection; some mechanically-improved devices may be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Recent cases considered whether such works 'should be copyrighted or patented'; nothing new except that 'a patent has just been sustained for an improved "check-book."' The distinction between utilitarian functional design (patent) and literary/artistic expression (copyright) is implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of book titles
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency is that copyright protects a title only as part of the substantial work, and not the mere title itself; trade-mark law provides the available protection for titles distinct from content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English cases suggest: (1) a title has 'no special protection by the copyright law' except as part of the work; (2) using the same title without imitating the book or deceiving the public cannot be stopped by copyright; (3) appropriating a title to deceive purchasers is 'a fraud on the public' actionable independent of copyright law. Example disputes: 'Post-Office Directory' and 'Splendid Misery' cases; U.S. case where 'Irving's Works' could be used by others once copyright expired because public not misled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' rights to name attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer shall not be compelled to furnish manuscript which he withholds because he knows it will be published under another man's name in a way to deceive the public; the right to have one's own name appear after an outright sale is a separate legal question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case: An author (Marsh) refused to deliver manuscript when publisher planned to publish under another's name (Kenny); court decided in favor of the author. Distinguish contractual terms and whether author sold rights outright.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in dramatic works (plays and operas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright of a play (drama, opera) is not infringed unless 'some substantial, material part — more than a new mode of representing a couple of matters not really essential to the unity of the plot — has been taken.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: House of Lords decision on two rival dramatizations of Eugene Sue's 'The Wandering Jew' held that taking two striking scenographic scenes from one dramatization by another was not enough to constitute infringement. Also: when two or more persons jointly own the copyright of an opera or drama, one cannot represent it or license a manager to do so without consent of the others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in musical compositions and arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical compositions are fully entitled to protection; an arranger may obtain copyright in his arrangement even though he is not the original composer of the underlying foreign work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An 'arrangement' of a French waltz copyrighted and protected against republishing of substantially the same arrangement. The judge said 'a man need not be an original author — the sole creator of the work; the first publisher could fairly get a copyright for his arrangement.' But copying the foreign original (if legitimately obtained) may, in some circumstances, be a defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in pictorial works and portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictorial works may be protected, but pictures whose chief element is a portrait of a living person are problematic as subjects of copyright; protection depends on originality and the prominence of accessory elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Earthenware ornamented with a portrait copied from a photograph and a portrait painted 'in character' — decisions suggest 'a picture of a living person is not a proper subject-matter of copyright' when the design's chief element is the portrait and accessories are trivial. Contrast: where designs were drawn by the artist (John Leech) on blocks, the artist retained the copyright; disputes over ownership of physical blocks versus design were resolved by considering dealings and the relative value of the designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of engraving copyright vs applied patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright in an engraving protects prints and other works 'adapted to be sold and used as engravings' (works meant to please the eye), but not patterns produced for different practical purposes (e.g., embroidery guides), since purposes differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The Huguenot' engraving adapted as a chromolithograph pattern for Berlin-wool work was held not to infringe the engraving copyright because the pattern served a different purpose than the picture; the pattern bought from Germany was not regarded as a copy in the copyright sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright in maps, charts, and practical patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Copyright protects the exact multiplication of copies; it does not grant exclusive rights to arbitrary signs, keys, or methods of exhibiting information so that another map drawn on the same plan for a different locality is not a copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Insurance maps using novel systems of colors and signs were held not to be infringed by similar maps of a different city. A dealer's card showing paint hues was held not to be a chart subject to copyright; pattern-prints with cutting lines and embroidery guides were said to be 'not the subject of copyright.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of unpublished lectures retained for repeated delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: A lecturer who does not print but retains addresses for repeated oral delivery has a right to control their publication; courts have recognized such a lecturer's right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference: Article titled 'Medical Lectures and the Law of Copyright' narrated a decision in favor of a lecturer's right; rumor that question to be raised again in a suit by Colonel Ingersoll.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability of importers, partners, and employers for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An importer is bound to ascertain whether imported books contain material he is not allowed to sell; importing without inquiry takes the risk. Conversely, in some American decisions a partner or employer is not chargeable with statutory penalty for copyright violations committed by a partner or agent without his authority or knowledge — intent must be shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: London publishers prosecuted an importer selling American paper containing English extracts — court held importer must ascertain contents. American decision held that 'some intention to violate the law must be shown' to sustain penal prosecution of a partner or employer for unauthorized acts by an agent.
